Foreword 


This Yizkor book of the Sephardic Jews of Bitola, Yugoslavia, is surely the most obscure 
Holocaust memorial book ever produced. Until now, it has not been found in any Yizkor book 
collection in the United States. There are no mentions of it in bibliographies of such books, and it 
has even eluded the notice of the eminent Jewish librarian Zachary Baker, whose list of memorial 
volumes is the standard in the field. The bibliographic record at the Yad Vashem archives, which 
holds the only known manuscript copy of the book, also offers no clue as to its identity. The entry 
does not identify it as a Yizkor book. Instead, it is described as a History of the Jewish Community 
of Bitola (Toldot kehilat yehudit Bitola). The only explicit mention of the book is found in the 
obscure 1971 volume A Town Called Monastir, which is a portrait of the Bitola Jews that calls the 
town by 1ts Ottoman Turkish name (and the one commonly used by its Jews). But even that book 
does not give the Yizkor book's title, nor does it tell where it could be found. This book, which 
memorializes more than 3,000 Jews, was itself for years lost and forgotten. 


Origins 

At the end of World War IT, Jacob Aroesti was one of the few Bitola Jews to survive the 
Holocaust. The city's Spanish-speaking Sephardim, descendants of the Jews who had settled in the 
town shortly after their expulsion from Spain in 1492, were deported to Treblinka in the spring of 
1943. The most reliable account of the community's destruction, The Jews in Macedonia During 
the Second World War, determined that the Nazis murdered 3,276 Bitola Jews, which was virtually 
100 per cent of the community. Only a few dozen people were able to evade deportation and 
escape into Bitola's surrounding mountains, where some survived as Partisan fighters. About 60 
Jews returned to Bitola after the war only to find that all of the city's Jewish institutions had been 
destroyed. Most of the returning Jews soon left. 

Jacob Aroesti decided to stay. Before the war, Aroesti had been an official of the Bitola Jewish 
community, and he appears to have overseen charitable programs the community maintained to 
alleviate poverty. According to Zamila Kolonomos, a Bitola Jew and historian who today lives in 
the neighboring city of Skopje, before the war Aroesti had dealings with nearly everyone in the 
Jewish community and was known for his excellent memory. After the war, and until his death in 
1960, Aroesti continued his work on behalf of the Bitola Jews. He was employed by the Bitola 
Archives to establish a record group called “The Jews in Bitola, 1860 — 1960.” 

To produce this book, Aroesti joined forces with two Macedonian brothers and researchers, 
Milos and Dusko Konstantinov. Aroesti and the Konstantinovs found their sources in pre-war 
Jewish community records, as well as a register of the adult Jewish population that was compiled 
in 1942 in preparation for the Jews’ deportation. Using those documents, the three men in 1959 
produced this book, entitled Bitoljski Jevreji (Bitolj's Jews). Its 865 pages include a 57-page 
introduction and 808 pages of biographical entries on 3,762 Bitola Jews, which was the number 
the writers believed had been killed in the Holocaust. It is written in Serbo-Croatian, with the first 
half in the Cyrillic alphabet and the remainder written in the Latin alphabet. 

The book was never published. Only two typed copies of it were ever produced. 


Rediscovery 


In 1997, when I began researching my history of the Bitola-Monastir Jews, I found mention of 
this memorial volume in A Town Called Monastir. In my determination to find it, I contacted the 


Bitola Archives and the Jewish Federation of Belgrade, Yugoslavia. The latter was able to confirm 
that such a book did exist, but had become lost. Years before, one copy had been sold to someone 
in the United States. No record of the sale was kept. The second copy, according to the last 
surviving author, Dusko Konstantinov, was deposited with the Belgrade Jewish Community. But 
Belgrade did not have it. My search quickly came to a dead end. 

By October 2000, I was close to completing my research when I received a response to an 
inquiry I had submitted to the Yad Vashem archives. It was a list of manuscript items regarding 
the Bitola Jews. The History of the Jewish Community of Bitola had been highlighted by the 
archivist, who wrote next to it in the margin, “988 pages.” The girth caught my eye. Yizkor books 
commonly tip the scales at close to 900 pages. I soon confirmed that it was the lost Yizkor book. 


Mute Testimony 

In many ways, this Yizkor book is similar to the many hundreds of others that commemorate 
the communities destroyed in the Holocaust. Like all memorial books, the overwhelming 
majority of its pages are devoted to preserving the names of the dead. Here, each family unit is 
given an individually numbered subhead, under which is an entry for each member of the family. 
Biographical details almost always include date and place of birth, and sometimes much more. 
For example, the entry for Mordo Nahmias, on page 573, takes up three-quarters of a page and 
mentions the years he lived Belgrade, his return to Bitola, and his membership in Yugoslavia's 
communist party. 

The book's introduction also resembles what is found in other Yizkor books. There is a history 
of the community, which in this Sephardic case includes the story of the Golden Age 
of Spain and its flourishing Jewish life, Spain's expulsion of the Jews, and their arrival in the 
Ottoman Empire, which ruled much of southeastern Europe, including Bitola. There is also 
information about prominent rabbis of the community, 20!" century charitable organizations, and 
a proud assertion that when the false messiah Sabbetai Zevi caused many 17" century Ottoman 
Jews to believe that the age of redemption had arrived, the Jews of Bitola refused to swerve away 
from normative Jewish practice. 

But despite these similarities, this book is unusual in a disturbing way. What is most striking is 
the complete absence of any Jewish symbols, Hebrew lettering, or Jewish language. There is no 
Star of David, no Hebrew, and no Judeo-Spanish, which was the native language of the Bitola Jews. 
It is a book cut off from its past and its community. The Serbo-Croatian language and Cyrillic 
alphabet made it unintelligible to the 3,000 Bitola-Monastir Jews who had emigrated to the United 
States in the early 20' century, when the city was under Ottoman rule. At that time, the Jews 
spoke Judeo-Spanish at home, learned French at the Alliance Israélite Universelle schools, and 
spoke Greek in the marketplace. The Bitola Jews who emigrated to Israel in the 1930s, when the 
city was under Yugoslav rule, had indeed received their early schooling in Serbo-Croat. But by 
1959, Hebrew would have been a better way to reach out to them. 

Instead, the choice of Serbo-Croatian seems to indicate a despair in finding an audience. Itis a 
book that expects no readers. It seems less a literate communication than a mute sign, a tomb 
stone for thousands. 


—Mark Cohen 


Mark Cohen is the author of Last Century of a Sephardic Community: The Jews of Monastir, 1839-1943.
